q: Matter is made up of tiny particles, which can be atoms or molecules.
e: The textbook states that all substances are matter and matter is made up of tiny particles, which can be atoms or molecules.

q: Plasma is a hot ionised gas containing charged particles.
e: Plasma is recognized as a fourth state of matter, described as a hot ionised gas containing charged particles.

q: The particles in a solid are packed very tightly together with weak forces between one another.
e: The particles in a solid are packed very tightly together with strong forces between one another.

q: Solids have a definite shape and volume.
e: Because particles in a solid have little freedom of movement and vibrate about a fixed position, solids have a definite shape and volume.

q: Unlike gases, solids cannot be compressed and do not flow.
e: These are common properties of all solids due to the strong forces holding their particles in fixed positions.

q: Solids do not expand when heated.
e: Solids do expand slightly when heated as the particles vibrate more strongly.

q: Liquids are composed of particles which are fixed in definite positions as in solids.
e: Liquids are composed of particles which are not fixed in any definite positions, allowing them to move freely throughout the liquid.

q: Liquids can have a definite volume because the particles in liquid are held together more strongly than those in gases.
e: The stronger attractive forces in liquids compared to gases allow them to maintain a definite volume.

q: Unlike gases, liquids cannot be compressed but they can flow easily.
e: Liquids cannot be compressed due to particle proximity, but they can flow easily because particles are not fixed in position.

q: The particles in a gas are in constant and rapid motion because of strong attractive forces between gaseous particles.
e: The particles in a gas are in constant and rapid motion because of weak attractive forces between gaseous particles.

q: Gases do not have a definite volume and shape of their own.
e: Gas particles move freely and spread out to occupy the whole space of the container, taking its shape and volume.

q: All gases can easily be compressed and spread in all directions.
e: Due to weak attractive forces and large spaces between particles, all gases can easily be compressed and spread in all directions.

q: Brownian motion is the continuous random movement of small particles suspended in a gas or liquid.
e: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the gas or liquid particles, such as the motion of pollen grains on still water.

q: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the solid container walls only.
e: Brownian motion arises from collisions with the gas or liquid particles, not just the container walls.

q: Diffusion is mainly seen in solids and liquids.
e: Diffusion is mainly seen in liquids and gases, where particles have more freedom of movement.

q: In diffusion, the particles of one substance mix with and move through the particles of another substance.
e: This is the exact definition of the diffusion process as described in the textbook.

q: The bigger the mass of particles, the faster the particles diffuse.
e: The bigger the mass, the slower the particles diffuse; the smaller the mass, the faster they diffuse.

q: The higher the temperature, it enables the particles to diffuse faster.
e: Higher temperatures provide particles with more kinetic energy, enabling them to diffuse faster.

q: The air, the sea water, and alloys are pure substances.
e: The air, sea water, and alloys are not pure substances; they are mixtures.

q: Adding sugar to tea or coffee is a solid-liquid mixture.
e: This process involves a solid (sugar) mixing with a liquid (tea or coffee), forming a solid-liquid mixture.
